facts.statement: Aurornis lived about 10 million years before Archaeopteryx, the species often considered the earliest bird.
facts.quote: The fossil evidence for the animal pre-dates that of Archaeopteryx lithographica, often considered the earliest bird species, by about 10 million years.

facts.statement: The species Aurornis xui was first described and named in 2013 by a team led by Pascal Godefroit.
facts.quote: Aurornis xui was first described and named by Pascal Godefroit, Andrea Cau, Hu Dong-Yu, François Escuillié, Wu Wenhao and Gareth Dyke in 2013.

facts.statement: Aurornis possessed clawed wings and a long bony tail.
facts.quote: It had clawed wings and a long bony tail.

facts.statement: While Aurornis had leg bones similar to Archaeopteryx, its overall anatomy was more primitive.
facts.quote: Its leg bones were similar to those of Archaeopteryx, but overall its anatomy was more primitive.

facts.statement: Fossil evidence shows traces of downy feathers on Aurornis's tail, chest, and neck.
facts.quote: The fossil features traces of downy feathers along the animal's tail, chest, and neck.

facts.statement: Analysis confirmed Aurornis came from the Tiaojishan Formation, dated to the late Jurassic (Oxfordian stage) approximately 160 million years ago.
facts.quote: Subsequent analysis confirmed it came from the Tiaojishan Formation, which has been dated to the late Jurassic period (Oxfordian stage), approximately 160 million years ago.

facts.statement: A 2014 analysis by Brusatte et al. recovered Aurornis outside Avialae, classifying it as a troodontid closely related to Anchiornis.
facts.quote: On the other hand, a phylogenetic analysis conducted by Brusatte et al. (2014) recovered Aurornis outside Avialae; it was recovered as a troodontid closely related to Anchiornis, Xiaotingia and Eosinopteryx.

facts.statement: A 2017 re-evaluation of the Harlem Archaeopteryx specimen found Aurornis to be an anchiornithid.
facts.quote: In 2017 re-evaluation of the Harlem Archaeopteryx specimen, Aurornis is found to be an anchiornithid.

facts.statement: Aurornis is classified within the unranked family Avialae.
Aurornis belongs to the family Anchiornithidae.
The absence of large feathers suggests that Aurornis xui was incapable of flight.
facts.quote: La ausencia de grandes plumas sugiere que A. xui era incapaz de volar.

facts.statement: The species name A. xui honors the paleontologist Xu Xing.
facts.quote: El nombre de la especie, A. xui, honra al paleontólogo Xu Xing.

facts.statement: Fossil remains of Aurornis have been found in the Tiaojishan Formation of Liaoning, China.
facts.quote: Sus restos fósiles han aparecido en la Formación Tiaojishan de Liaoning, China.

facts.statement: A 2013 phylogenetic analysis placed Aurornis within the avian lineage, in a position more basal than Archaeopteryx.
facts.quote: Un análisis filogenético de Aurornis publicado en 2013 encontró que pertenecía al linaje de las aves, en una posición más basal que la de Archaeopteryx.

facts.statement: The classification of A. xui as a bird is controversial because there are multiple different definitions of the word "bird".
facts.quote: La clasificación de A. xui como un ave es, sin embargo, materia de controversia, debido a que hay varias definiciones diferentes de la palabra "ave".

facts.statement: Paleontologist Luis Chiappe argued that the forelimb of A. xui is too short to be that of a true bird.
facts.quote: El paleontólogo Luis Chiappe dijo que el miembro delantero de A. xui es demasiado corto como para ser de un ave verdadera.

facts.statement: A 2017 study suggested that Aurornis might be a junior synonym of Anchiornis because its traits fall within Anchiornis's range of variation.
facts.quote: Un estudio de especímenes del avialano Anchiornis publicado en 2017 encontró que los rasgos que muestra Aurornis caen dentro del rango de variación de Anchiornis, lo que indicaría que es su sinónimo más moderno.

facts.statement: Aurornis lived from the Bathonian to the Kimmeridgian stages, between 168.2 and 152.21 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Bathonian to Kimmeridgian (168.2 to 152.21 million years ago)
